analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "... Mr. Pincus, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. The Federal Government disburses billions of dollars to state and local governments pursuant to a variety of grant programs. A recipient of such a Federal grant must agree to abide by statutory and regulatory requirements designed to ensure that the grant will further the goals of the Federal program. And the relevant statute typically provides that a grant recipient must repay to the Federal Government any funds spent in violation of those statutory and regulatory requirements. This authority to recoup unlawfully spent Federal funds generally serves as the Federal Government's principal method of enforcing compliance with these grant requirements and thereby ensuring that grant funds are used by recipients in a manner that furthers the public interest. This case concerns the Government's ability to utilize this enforcement authority with respect to grants under the Comprehensive Employment and Training Act, generally known as CETA. The specific question presented here is whether a procedural statute establishing a time limit for agency action should be interpreted to cut off the Federal Government's authority to recover unlawfully dispersed grant funds and thereby immunize grant recipients from this obligation to repay such funds to the United States. The CETA funds that are specifically the subject of this action were expended by respondent during the years 1974 to 1977. CETA was a Federal program designed to increase employment opportunities for economically disadvantaged persons. The Secretary of Labor dispersed funds to States and localities who operated employment programs, and the States and localities in turn agreed that their programs would comport with the requirements set forth in the Federal statute and the regulations promulgated by the Secretary. Department of Labor officials conducted two separate audits of respondents' expenditures of CETA grant funds. The audits uncovered some irregularities, and pursuant to the applicable regulations, the audit reports were transmitted for further review to the grant officer who administered respondents' grants. It is the receipt of these audit reports by the grant officer that provides the basis for respondents' invocation of the statutory provision that is an issue in this case. This provision, Section 106B of the CETA statute, states that the Secretary of Labor shall issue a final determination within 120 days of the receipt of a complaint alleging the unlawful use of CETA funds by a grant recipient. Here, the grant officer did not issue a final determination with respect to the information uncovered in the audits until more than 28 months after his receipt of the reports. The grant officer found that certain of respondents' expenditures violated CETA requirements, principally because the respondent had used the Federal funds to hire persons who were ineligible under the Federal standards of the CETA program. The grant officer, therefore, ordered respondent to repay to the United States an amount equal to the misspent grant funds. Respondent appealed the grant officer's determination to an administrative law judge, pursuant to the scheme set forth in the statute and regulations. And in addition to challenging the grant officer's substantive determination about the propriety of its expenditure of funds, respondent claimed that the grant officer's repayment order was invalid because it was not issued within the 120-day time period set forth in Section 106B. Now, the administrative law judge specifically addressed this claim and found that respondent had suffered no prejudice because of the delay in issuing the repayment order. It, therefore, rejected respondent's claim that Section 106B rendered the repayment order invalid, and the administrative law judge himself issued an order directing respondent to repay a total of $373,000, the amount of grant funds that he determined to have been expended in violation of the substantive rules of the CETA program. Mr. Pincus, may I ask what the government's position would be if the ALJ had found prejudice? Well, Your Honor, in our reply brief, we discussed that problem to some extent. Let me state as a preliminary matter that it seems quite unlikely that any prejudice could be found simply because of the way the process operates. The grant recipient gets notice that when, at the same time that the grant officer gets the audit report, the grant recipient gets notice that there are some irregularities that are being questioned, and, therefore, at that initial date, he's on notice that he should be preserving documents and preparing his case. Say there was an earthquake or something and they lost the document. Would you answer my question? Sure. No, I'm sorry. I was going to come to that. If there is a showing of prejudice and if there is no excuse for the Secretary's delay, we think that in an appropriate case that some either the withdrawal of the repayment order or some other equitable adjustment of the remedy might be appropriate. Of course, we think that the appropriate test probably is a test similar to the Barker against Wingo, or a four-factor test that looks to the length of the delay, the reasons for the delay, whether or not the grant recipient, in this case, has invoked any right that he might have to a speedy determination. And if a balancing of those factors indicates that there is prejudice, then we think some adjustment would be appropriate. The Ninth Circuit reversed the administrative law judge's determination and held that Section 106B prohibited the Secretary from recovering misspent CETA grant funds whenever a final determination is not issued within 120 days. The Court of Appeals rested its conclusion upon what it viewed as the plain meaning of the statute. It observed that Section 106B states that the Secretary shall issue a final determination within 120 days and concluded that the simple use of the term shall barred any subsequent issuance of a repayment order. The Court of Appeals rejected the Secretary's argument that the legislative history of Section 106B showed that Congress did not intend to impose any limitation upon the Secretary's enforcement authority. Now, we submit that each of the Court of Appeals' conclusions is demonstrably incorrect. Both the language used by Congress in drafting Section 106B and the relevant legislative history make clear beyond any doubt that this provision should not be interpreted to limit the Secretary's authority to recover unlawfully spent federal funds. Indeed, three Courts of Appeals, including the Eighth Circuit in a decision that was issued last week, have agreed with our position regarding the proper interpretation of Section 106B. The Ninth Circuit's basic error was its failure to correctly identify the question of statutory interpretation that is presented here. The Court of Appeals found that the 120 day time limit was mandatory and then assumed, without making any further inquiry, that the effect of the time limit was to restrict the Secretary's enforcement authority. But even when a time limit relating to government action is mandatory, rather than simply directory, there remains a second inquiry. It's necessary to determine the proper remedy for the government's failure to comply with that time limitation. In our view, Section 106B should be read to confer upon interested parties a right to an expeditious determination regarding the propriety of the grant officer's expenditures, a right which could be enforced by obtaining an order from an administrative law judge, for example, directing the grant officer to issue his final determination expeditiously where the grant officer has failed to act within 120 days. We think it's plain that Congress did not intend the remedy to be the cutting off of the government's right to recover unlawfully spent funds simply because the Secretary did not act within the relevant time period. Now, Section 106B, of course, is silent regarding the appropriate remedy in the event the Secretary fails to act in a timely manner. But this Court's decisions and a long line of decisions in the Courts of Appeals make clear that this silence itself is dispositive of the question of the appropriate remedy. The Court frequently has observed that statutes should be interpreted to protect the public interest against the consequences of delay by public officials, and it's refused to construe statutory time limits to bar actions commenced by the United States, for example, unless there's a clear indication that Congress intended that result. And the practical common sense of such a rule is quite obvious. Congress often attempts to spur agencies to quicker action by including in a statute a requirement that regulations be issued in a certain number of days or that another type of administrative determination be made within a specified period. It was certainly unsuccessful here, wasn't it, in spurring the Labor Department any quick action? Well, unfortunately, Your Honor, by 1978, when Section 106B was enacted, the Labor Department was already so far behind that it was—they had a long backlog to catch up with before they could even begin to process new actions in a timely manner. Unfortunately, the burdens of a lot of complaints and a lot of audit results and the lack, perhaps, of sufficient staff just made it impossible for the Secretary to comply with this time limitation in many cases. Mr. Pincus, can I ask—I know there are a lot of cases that say that unless the statute of limitations expressly applies to the government, we don't read that in. And here, of course, it clearly does apply to the government. And your argument, rather, is that they didn't specify a remedy for failure to meet the time plan, and there's a general rule that then there's no remedy, I guess, or no significant remedy. What is the case that most directly supports that argument that you rely on, the strongest authority you have for that proposition? A case in this Court, Your Honor? Yes. Well, I think there's no case in this Court that directly—cided by this Court that directly supports that proposition. I guess the cases that are closest to this Court's decisions in Wirtz and the Wheeland case and the St. Paul Railroad case, because in those cases, it was clear that Congress had enacted a statute of limitations, and the question was what the scope of the limitations—either what actions would be encompassed within the statute of limitations. No, I put that group to one side, because here we have clear—it's clear that the statute does apply to the government. And my question is, and the basic argument you make, as I understand it, is yes, but they didn't tell us what the consequence of the failure to comply with the deadline was. And you say if they don't tell us the consequence, you can ignore the statute. And I'm just wondering if there was really any authority for that argument. Well, Your Honor, we don't say that they can ignore the statute. There's a different remedy available for the government's failure to comply. What is the remedy for the failure to comply here? The remedy would be an injunction from an administrative law judge directing the government to act expeditiously. Please sue us. Please start the proceedings to recover money from us. Well, Your Honor, the remedy may seem a little odd in this circumstance, because as I'll discuss later in my argument, the purpose of Section 106B was not to protect grant recipients at all. It was to protect the people who filed complaints. And those people clearly would have an incentive to get an order to direct expeditious action. You don't think the grant recipients have any interest in knowing where they stand on these claims? Well, Your Honor, if they have such an interest, then they should invoke it. It's like the speedy trial clause questions. In a way, the invocation of a speedy trial right is a criminal defendant asking to be tried. But if the defendant wants to know where he stands, then he has to invoke his right. And this Court has said whether or not the defendant invokes his right is an important question in determining whether or not the right has been violated. And we think the same kind of analysis applies here. If the grant recipient is concerned about expeditious resolution, then the grant recipient has to spend it. Of course, the speedy trial analysis that you talk about is one where there's no specific deadline. When there's a deadline, it's a little different. Then they don't have the balancing of four or five factors. We think that the factors are relevant. In this Court's decision in 8850, it applied the Barker against Wingo tests to see how long delay is permissible, although there, too, there was not a specific deadline. But we think it's still appropriate in deciding what remedy is appropriate. I take it you have support in the Court's Appeals for your position? Yes, Your Honor. Both with respect to this particular statute, three Courts of Appeals have ruled in our favor. in respect to our general principle that statutory time limits on agency action do not cut off the government's authority in the absence of expressed consequences, a proposition that's been endorsed by a large number of Courts of Appeals. We'll resume there at 1 o'clock. Thank you. Mr. Pinkus, you may continue. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. As I discussed in my remarks before the lunch break and in my colloquy with Justice Stevens, we submit that the general principle underlying a number of this Court's decisions, that the public interest should not be sacrificed due to the negligence of government officers, itself supports our reading of Section 106B. However, the legislative history of the provision independently mandates the conclusion that Congress did not intend to limit the Secretary's enforcement authority by enacting the provision. And this conclusion is supported both by the specific legislative history of the provision and the general purposes of the 1978 SETA amendments that included Section 106B. With respect to Section 106B itself, the legislative history establishes that the provision was enacted to protect individuals who had filed complaints against grant recipients such as respondent. The 1973 SETA statute had authorized individuals employed in SETA programs, as well as other interested parties, to file complaints with the Secretary of Labor, alleging that a grant recipient had failed to comply with the applicable statutory or regulatory requirements. For example, an employee might allege that a grant recipient was paying improperly low wages. Congress found in 1978 that the Labor Department was not processing these complaints within a reasonable time, and that it therefore enacted the 120-day time limit in Section 106B to remedy this particular problem. Section 106B thus was designed to enable SETA program beneficiaries to enable to obtain a more expeditious resolution of their claims against grant recipients. But, Mr. Pincus, does the legislative history that you're referring to give any indication of what Congress thought should be done at the end of 120 days? Well, there is both specific legislative history regarding this question, and we think the general purpose compels the conclusion that we're supporting. First of all, the author of the language that became Section 106B, Congressman Obi, stated specifically in the House of Representatives that the Secretary's failure to comply or to act within 120 days did not remove the Secretary's jurisdiction to act in the matter. So we think that definitively resolves the question whether or not Section 106B eliminates the Secretary's enforcement authority. It simply doesn't. In addition, the contrary interpretation of Section 106B adopted by the Court of Appeals would turn the purpose of the provision on its head. Instead of protecting the rights of the complainants, Section 106B would extinguish their rights whenever the Secretary failed to act within 120 days. And neither the legislative history nor the purpose would justify such a perverse reading of the statute. Mr. Pinkus, Justice Rehnquist asked you if there was anything in the legislative history that indicated what was supposed to be done at the end of the 120 days. What's your answer to that question? What did they think the 120 days was supposed to require? Well, the provision requires the Secretary to act within 120 days. And if he doesn't act, what does the statute imply should be done? The statute is silent on the matter, and we think that Congressman Obie's comments and the purpose of the statute itself requires the conclusion that it would make no sense for the complainant's rights to be cut off. We think that a more appropriate remedy would be an order from an administrative law judge directing the Secretary to act to issue the final determination that had not been issued within the 120-day period. Do you have the power to issue that sort of an order to the Secretary? Well, he would be issuing the order to the Secretary's designee, to the grant officer, in this particular case. It's the Secretary's delegated to the grant officer the power to issue these final determinations. And we think that he could do that, and that, in fact, is what happened in the Milwaukee County case. The Secretary grant officer had failed to act on a complaint within 120 days. The complainant went to the administrative law judge, and the administrative law judge issued such an order, and the grant officer issued the final determination. And we think that is a more appropriate administrative procedure because it reconciles the interest in expedition with the interest in protecting complainant's rights and enforcing the requirements of the CETA statute. Are you saying that the purpose of the statute is to protect the right of the complainant, in effect, the private party? Because if you are, you cited the case of French against Edwards to us at page 12 of your brief and quoted one sentence out of the opinion, and then in the next sentence that talks about where the deadline is for the protection of the citizen, why then the direction should be mandatory. You didn't quote that language. Well, you are. I think we're confusing two different private parties. There is a complaint. There is a grant recipient who is, like Respondent here, the party that gets the money from the federal government. And then there is a party that files a complaint alleging that such a grant recipient has misused federal funds. So we think that Section 106B plainly was enacted to protect the rights of complainants, not to protect the rights of grant recipients, such as respondents. Because Congress was responding to the problem that complaints had not been acted on within a timely fashion. It wasn't concerned about the question of whether or not grant recipients might be prejudiced by that delay. It was concerned about whether the complainants, the employees of people like grant recipients, were prejudiced because their claims weren't being acted upon in a timely fashion. Is there some sort of a quetam or informer provision regarding these potential plaintiffs who are going to file complaints about the use of cedar funds? I'm sorry, Justice Rehnquist. I'm not familiar with that. Well, something whereby they get a certain percentage of what's recovered. I'm not familiar with such a provision, but in many cases the complaints would be to enforce their own rights. For example, in the situation where the employee of a grant recipient was being paid low wages, that employee might file a complaint with the Secretary because his own wages should be set at a higher level. But he would benefit in that way. He would benefit because he would get an award of that back compensation and a future adjustment in his salary. So I think it's crucial to understand this. I must confess, I find it hard to envision that kind of case. Usually the Federal Government is trying to get money back from State or Municipal Governments. And how would they get government money back if they'd been underpaying somebody? I just don't understand that example. Well, let me step back for a second, Justice Stevens. There are two possible types of administrative actions that can be prosecuted against grant recipients. An individual, in one case, an individual such as an employee of the grant recipient can file a complaint alleging that the grant recipient has done something wrong and that that particular individual has been harmed in some way. That would be the example of the policeman who was being paid with CETA funds but was getting a wage that was impermissibly low under the Federal statute standards. And that kind of case would not give rise to a recovery of funds action by the Federal Government, I don't suppose. In that kind of a case, the recovery would go to the particular complainant who had been wronged. That's the kind of case that Section 106B is designed to deal with. There is a separate kind of case where, after the grant recipient has spent its money, its expenditures are audited by a Federal Government or a private order, and some irregularities may be found. And the question is whether the Federal Government may recover those misspent Federal funds. That's the kind of a case that is at issue here. And we think it makes no sense to interpret Section 106B in this context any differently than in the other context. It shouldn't cut off the right to enforce CETA's provisions against the grant recipient. But, Mr. Pincus, apparently the Secretary's own regulations say that an audit report triggers the 120-day period, even though it isn't a complainant, as you have described. So do we defer to the Secretary's interpretation then? Well, Your Honor, we don't think that the Court has to decide here, and we haven't presented the question, whether Section 106B actually applies only to complaints or applies to both audits and complaints. We think, assuming the question, rather, is what the effect of a violation of Section 106B is in either situation, and we think the effect is the same in both contexts. It doesn't cut off the complainant's rights to get a remedy, and it doesn't cut off the Secretary's right to recover misspent Federal funds. It rather gives both the complainant, in one case, and the grant recipient, in the other case, the right to obtain a more expeditious processing of the complaint or the audit result. And as I mentioned before, Congress itself expressly considered this question of what the appropriate remedy should be for a violation of Section 106B, and specified that the provision did not limit the Secretary's enforcement authority. You say Congress. You don't mean that Congress itself did that. There's legislative history supporting the view that some congressmen thought that was what you did. But a congressman, who was the author of this particular language, stated that in a colloquy with the floor manager of the House bill, and that's legislative history that the Court has said in previous opinions is entitled to a considerable weight. And we think that's especially so here because there isn't any contradictory legislative history as to what the proper remedy for a violation of Section 106B should be. And because that comment fits so closely with the purpose of the provision, again, it wouldn't make any sense that the remedy for the Secretary's failure to comply with a provision that is supposed to protect complainants would be to dismiss the complainant's claim. And that's essentially, that is the construction of Section 106B that respondent contends for. And we don't think that Congress could possibly have intended that result. Finally, just a word about the general purpose of the 1978 CETA amendments, which also supports our conclusion. Those amendments in general were designed to strengthen the Secretary's enforcement authority. The legislative history is replete with comments, both the committee reports and in the debates on the floor, that Congress wanted CETA requirements to be applied more strictly to grant recipients. And it would be inconsistent to interpret Section 106B in a manner that would handicap the Secretary's enforcement efforts and provide grant recipients with a windfall by protecting them from their obligation to pay what are clearly unlawfully spent federal funds. For these reasons, we think that the Court of Appeals erred and the judgment of the Court of Appeals should be reversed. May I ask just one other question? Because I'm just still a little having trouble visualizing the claim of the complainant who wants some money of some kind, an underpaid police officer or something like that. Who would be his adversary in a proceeding? His adversary. The way the program works is the grants are given to an entity such as Pierce County who then hires the policeman. Right. And then who would the policeman be suing? He would be filing a complaint against Pierce County. Well, that really doesn't go to the question whether the Secretary can plead the 120-day. I mean, the Secretary can avoid compliance for 120 days. I just—the cases we're dealing with are cases where the United States government is going against a local governmental unit trying to recover funds that were misused. I don't understand why— Well, Your Honor, the 120-day sentence in Section 106b by its terms applies only to those kind of— Well, I understand, but it's just so counterpointed that your regulations make it applicable to this case. Yes, but we think the effect of the provision should be considered by reference to what Congress's purpose, what Congress was thinking about when it enacted the provision, and what Congress was thinking about were those kind of complaints filed by the underpaid policeman. I mean, since it couldn't have meant to cut off those complaints— Well, we don't have before us the question whether the failure of the Secretary to act promptly in response to an underpaid policeman's claim would bar his claim six or eight months later. That just—there's nothing in the statute that suggests that. But— The question is whether the Secretary's own failure to act barred the Secretary's claim. But, Your Honor, the basis for the claim that our enforcement action is barred is this same 120-day provision that applies only to complaints. Yeah, but I don't know how you could reasonably say that the Secretary's failure to act would bar a policeman's claim. That's what I— Because— Well, Your Honor, because if the Secretary's failure to act barred the Secretary's claim, that would be based on the 120-day rule that is set forth in Section 106B. Correct. Since that very sentence applies the 120-day rule to complaints, it would of necessity bar any further action on a complaint. There's no way to distinguish the two situations. Except that—well, all right, I understand your argument. I'd like to reserve the balance of my time. Mr. Kram. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. I would like to state a few facts before I delve into the issues. In this case, there was a mention of irregularities in the Solicitor General's argument, so I think perhaps we need to say a little bit more about the allegations of irregularities. It's been said in the last many years that the CETA program was rife with abuses and rife with fraud. And this case comes before you today after a petition for certiorari in which it was stated that there are $72 million in federal funds that would be barred, according to the government, if you were to rule in favor of Pierce County. So I think it's important to mention in that context that in controversy here is $375,000 of federal grants, given in two federal grants, one of which was a smaller one of about $110,000 disallowed, and the other one was $265,000. But in neither of those grants were there any issues of fraud or the kinds of abuses that we hear about so frequently in these cases. These were irregularities more in the nature of technicalities or in the nature of eligibility violations or failures to maintain documents. And it's very important, I think, for us to realize that the specifics of this case show the reason for the rule. The seven jailers whose wages were disallowed, their wages that were paid over those three or four years where they continued to be employed by Pierce County, were paid to them in spite of the fact that they were not unemployed for 15 days before they began to participate. As it came out through the administrative law judge process and all of the hearings, it was admitted by all parties that they had indeed been unemployed for 15 days, but the local officials had decided that they were eligible prematurely on about the seventh or eighth day. So we're not dealing with cases where people were clearly ineligible for this federal program. What is that distinction again, Counsel? You say it was contended that they were ineligible because they had not been unemployed for 15 days? Yes, Your Honor. In this particular program, it's a public service employment Title VI CETA grant, and under the applicable regulations, one has to be unemployed for 15 days before they begin to participate. And the administrative law judge agreed with Pierce County that participate means to actually begin earning wages. However, Pierce County was still liable because they had prematurely decided that these gentlemen were ineligible on approximately the seventh day of the 15-day period. Well, now, you say they had prematurely decided that they were ineligible or eligible? No, eligible, Your Honor, because how could one know that the other participant would be indeed still unemployed at the end of the 15-day period if one made the determination on the seventh day? So they took them into the program when they had been unemployed only seven days? They applied and were accepted into the program on about the seventh day. It varied, actually. Well, you can say that they were prematurely taken in, but they were taken in at a time they weren't qualified under the rule, weren't they? Right, but they were, Your Honor, people that were specifically let go and then rehired by Pierce County with the understanding by us that they would indeed be unemployed for that statutory period. I just mention it because it's so... Well, so they had been employed by Pierce County, and then they were let go for 15 days and then rehired so they could come in under CETA? Well, Your Honor, there was, in fact, a maintenance of effort claim earlier in the case, and it dropped by the wayside at the administrative law judge level. That means maintenance of effort is the concept that federal grant monies shall be used to supplement rather than supplant your local funds. and the administrative law judge, based upon the evidence, made a finding that these people would, in fact, have been laid off by Pierce County because of the budget problems that we had at the time, January of 1975. He was satisfied, under all the evidence, that there was no maintenance of effort and there was no paper layoff, that there were legitimate rehires. But what he said was, you're still liable because there's a technical violation. And that's all I wanted to point out to the Court was the nature of the alleged violations. The second thing I wanted to point out about these grants, factually, is that one of the grants was what we call a conduit grant, where the money was merely passed through Pierce County, in part, not in its entirety, but some of the participants were not even employees of Pierce County as public service employees. They were either private sector or other public sector employees, and all Pierce County did was do the intake processing, as we call it, the personnel work, and then referred them to the school district or the private industry that accepted them for unemployment. So, and I think that becomes relevant later on when you think about the equities of the case, that they were not even, in other words, the money of their wages did not even go to Pierce County, in some cases. But the recovery by the federal government would be from Pierce County? Solely from Pierce County at this point, Your Honor, because- And I suppose Pierce County could try to recover, in turn, from the actual users of the people hired? That's my point, Your Honor. And even mentioning the conduit theory is that, no, we would indeed not now be able to recover because the State Statute of Limitations would have run. The beginning of the period and the alleged violation in this case on the smaller audit was January of 1975. It's now 1986, and our State Statute of Limitations is six years. Our rights against those subgrantees have long since been foreclosed. And did Pierce County make any effort in this case to compel the federal government to go ahead and issue its audit report by seeking such an order of mandamus-type order from an administrative law judge? No, Your Honor. Why not? We did not. And, first of all, I don't think there is any such mandamus remedy under law. First of all, if you- But do you think, do you disagree with the Solicitor General's Office that Pierce County could have sought an order from an administrative law judge? Yes, Justice O'Connor, I do. There is no such procedure in the regulations. Furthermore, I do not think an administrative law judge has equitable jurisdiction to issue mandamus or injunctive relief. That is a remedy that's peculiar to the courts and is within their inherent power. But the administrative law judge agency wasn't even created until the 1979 amendments to the regulations. And to me, they were given no power to do that, and maybe there's a precedent for it, but I say that the remedy was created out of whole cloth by the Department of Labor. Well, equity was created out of whole cloth. At the time, they thought the common law courts were too harsh. I agree with that, Your Honor, but I think that there's a far cry and a great distance between an administrative law judge court or quasi-judicial body and a judicial body like this one or the constitutional courts of this country. So, actually, I think the purpose of 106B is not something that we differ on at all. The purpose of this statute was relatively clear from the legislative history. Congress intended to have the Department take prompt and decisive steps to remedy a perceived problem in this country in the CETA program. The problem was at two levels. It was at the recipient level, or what we sometimes refer to as the prime sponsor level, and it was acknowledged to be at the Department of Labor level. And when they passed 106B with respect to complaints, I believe that if you read the entire colloquy of the Obie Amendment, colloquy between Obie and Mr. Hawkins, Congressman Hawkins, that you will find that the insertion of the Obie Amendment probably related more to the complaint process. There's like a tripartite scheme in this. There's the grant officer, there's the administrative law judge, and then there's the courts.
